metadataReview.note: The cached Wikidata battle has no P625 and incorrectly links P276 to Munich (Q1726), whose city coordinate was inherited. Use the official Landkreis Regensburg point for Schloss Eggmühl, a documented fighting site in the battle of 22 April 1809. The municipal historical event description explicitly identifies the surviving castle wall as an assault site. This represents the castle sector of the larger battlefield; it does not define all troop positions or the battlefield perimeter. The date is unchanged. The municipal description was read in the search index; the original URL currently serves a generic page after a site migration.

metadataReview.coordinateBasis: Landkreis Regensburg publishes Schloss Eggmühl at Kirchplatz 1 with GeoCoordinates latitude 48.843923667897869 and longitude 12.183163404442897. Rounded to six decimals and stored longitude first. The castle is linked to actual fighting by the municipal historical account of its wall being stormed during the 22 April 1809 battle. This is an official site POI point, not a surveyed battle center, town centroid, memorial proxy, or inferred digit correction.

note:
Reviewed CDB90 match 124, pinned revision e0b35ec4d798cec3bb4e6970c0f6bb7aa69e2f4c. CDB90 (CAA Database of Battles, Version 1990), tidy data maintained by Jeffrey B. Arnold. Original US Army Concepts Analysis Agency data; revised data licensed ODC-BY. Original force designations and strength interpretations are retained with each quantity. Each side is one aggregate force, including any coalition; its total is not allocated among members. Personnel casualties are not deaths. Source estimates and adjudged error margins are not statistical confidence intervals. Equipment and tactical movements are not established by this dataset. Match review: Exact linked article, named engagement and complete source first/last day match the catalogue. The row is parentless, with no competing source row for this target. Preserve the two original source NAM force identities; counts remain CDB estimates.

The recorded French army in 1809–1814 receives the shako-and-musket infantry family. Musée de l’Armée documents the shako replacing the bicorne from 1806 and surviving 1813–1815 equipment; its evidence supports this later-period component without claiming uniform issue across every regiment or allied contingent. The model is a representative infantry component, not an exact regimental uniform or a statement that every soldier used that equipment. Coalition identities, component proportions, CDB 90 personnel evidence and all loss categories remain unchanged.
